timeline.title: We decided to visit the customer company and discover their bottlenecks.
timeline.description:
To bridge the persistent gap between reported symptoms and ground-level technical reality, we made the strategic decision to conduct an intensive on-site technical immersion at the customer’s facility.

While remote discovery calls and ticket logs capture surface friction, they routinely obscure the informal manual workarounds, fragmented data handoffs, and undocumented system constraints that operational teams navigate daily. By embedding our Forward-Deployed Engineers directly on the ground, we can observe live end-to-end workflows in real time rather than relying on second-hand assumptions or sanitized status reports.

Our objective during this visit is to execute a rigorous bottleneck discovery across three critical vectors: identifying friction points in legacy system integrations, mapping manual data-entry redundancies, and analyzing operational handoffs between frontline staff and back-office IT. Directly shadowing operators allows us to pinpoint precisely where throughput stalls, where systemic errors originate, and where architectural intervention provides the highest immediate leverage.

This immersion transitions our engagement from reactive firefighting to high-conviction, outcome-aligned engineering. Discovering root causes on-site establishes an authoritative baseline of truth, ensuring our Definition of Done solves genuine operational bottlenecks, accelerates time-to-value, and builds deep stakeholder trust.

Product Thinking
Training Session 1
02/10/2026
S Jeyaseelan
Founder, ExamBlue

The Product Journey
01
USER
02
GOAL
03
BEHAVIOR
04
PROBLEM
05
OPPORTUNITY
06
SOLUTION
Practical Application
We will map and analyze this sequential 
framework through a simple, everyday 
YouTube search scenario.
By examining concrete user steps rather than 
abstract theories, we establish a repeatable 
pattern for evidence gathering.
Core Objective
Learn strict evidence discipline without 
getting bogged down by overly complex 
frameworks.
Ensure all engineering and product 
decisions remain directly grounded in real, 
observable user needs.

User Journey: React Tutorial Search
Note: This is a hypothetical training scenario, not actual research data.
Consider a student who wants to learn React. They search for a "React project tutorial" and are presented 
with many results. They open several videos, watch parts of them, and leave some due to length or 
difficulty. Eventually, they find a useful video that matches their needs.
STEP 01
Search
User initiates a 
search for a "React 
project tutorial".
STEP 02
Many Results
Encounters and 
evaluates many 
search results 
presented.
STEP 03
Several 
Videos
Clicks on several 
videos, leaving some 
due to length or 
difficulty.
OUTCOME
Useful Video
Eventually discovers 
a useful video that 
perfectly matches 
their needs.

Understanding the User's Goal
Before analyzing the product or writing any code, we must fundamentally understand the user's goal by answering 
three core questions:
1. WHO is the user?
In our case study, it is a university student 
learning React at his motivation.
2. WHAT are they trying to 
accomplish?
They want to learn the basic concept of 
react and build a functional React project 
as a beginner.
3. WHY are they using the product?
They are actively searching for simpler, 
beginner friendly, practical, step-by-step 
guidance video.
Core Principle
Mastering these three questions ensures 
our foundation is built on human intent, 
not just system mechanics.

Deﬁning Observable User Behavior
Documenting objective screen actions before forming product hypotheses
01. SEARCH
User enters query 
"React project 
tutorial" in search bar.
02. EXPLORATION
Opens multiple video 
links in tabs and 
watches partial 
segments.
03. ABANDONMENT
Exits several videos 
early and executes a 
refined search query.
04. RESOLUTION
Selects, watches, and 
completes a useful 
video tutorial.
GOLDEN RULE: OBSERVATION ≠ ASSUMPTION
The foundation of product engineering requires separating objective telemetry from unverified speculation. 
We must strictly record raw behavioral data first.
✓ OBJECTIVE OBSERVATION (RAW TELEMETRY)
User navigated away after 45 seconds of playback 
and submitted a secondary search query.
✕ UNGROUNDED ASSUMPTION (DO NOT INVENT)
"The video quality was poor" or "The user found the 
speaker boring and lost interest."

Separating Facts from Hypotheses
Observation
"The student opened several videos 
before choosing one."
An undeniable record of what happened.
Possible Interpretation
"The student may have difficulty 
determining which video is relevant 
before watching it."
A hypothesis about why it might have happened.
THE GOLDEN RULE OF EVIDENCE-DRIVEN THINKING
Do not confuse what we know with what we think.
Maintaining this boundary prevents us from building solutions for the wrong root cause.

EXERCISE: EVIDENCE DISCIPLINE
Scenario
"A student searches 'React project tutorial' and opens five different videos 
before completing one."
You have 3 minutes to answer the following:
1. What do we strictly KNOW based on this statement?
2. What are we ASSUMING about the user's intent or frustration?
3. What additional data would we need to know to understand the behavior better?
Note: Do not design a solution yet. Focus entirely on practicing strict evidence discipline.

Tracing Behavior to the Real Problem
Behavior: "I opened five videos."
Possible Explanation: "I cannot easily determine which video is appropriate for 
my goal."
Deeper Issue: "I don't have enough information to evaluate relevance 
before investing time."
Key Takeaway: A user's behavior is not automatically their core problem. Opening five videos is 
merely an observed action; the lack of upfront visual/content context to evaluate relevance is the 
structural problem to solve.

Solution vs. User Problem
We must learn to distinguish between a proposed solution and a true user problem. Consider these 
two statements:
01. Proposed Solution
“I need an AI summary before 
watching a video.ˮ
This is a Proposed Solution disguised as a 
need.
02. Potential User Problem
“I have difficulty determining 
whether a video is relevant to my 
goal.ˮ
This is a Potential User Problem.
Core Principle
Our core principle is to fully understand the problem before accepting a solution. Jumping 
straight to the feature bypasses the critical step of validating the actual user friction.

EXERCISE: PROBLEM IDENTIFICATION
Scenario
A student searches for a specific programming topic. The search returns many videos. The student opens 
several videos because it is difficult to know which one matches their level and intended outcome.
Task (4 minutes)
Write down:
● The User goal
● The Observed behavior
● The Possible problem
Key Question to consider
"What specific evidence would we need to gather before becoming confident that this 
is actually a meaningful problem worth solving?"

Problem vs. Opportunity
Once we define the problem, we reframe it into an actionable opportunity.
Problem
Users may struggle to determine which 
content is relevant to their specific goal 
before clicking.
Opportunity
Make it easier for users to identify 
relevant content directly from the search 
results.
The Critical Distinction
A problem describes the difficulty the user is facing. An opportunity describes where the product 
could create value by removing that difficulty. Framing it as an opportunity opens the door for 
creative engineering.

End-to-End Framework Flow
We have finally reached the end of the flow: User goal → Observed behavior → Possible problem → Opportunity → Possible solution.
STEP 01
User Goal
STEP 02
Observed 
Behavior
STEP 03
Possible 
Problem
STEP 04
Opportunity
STEP 05 • SOLUTION
Possible Solution
An Example Solution: Provide 
clearer, upfront information that 
helps users determine whether a 
video matches their goal before 
they invest time watching it.
Caution
This is only one possible solution out of many. We should never assume our first idea is the 
correct one.
The solution must be tested against the evidence to ensure it actually addresses the identified 
opportunity.

Evaluating Solutions
1. IDENTIFY THE PROBLEM: Always begin by clearly defining the core user problem.
2. ASSESS LIMITATIONS: Ask if there is a fundamental limitation in existing approaches.
3. TEST NORMAL SOFTWARE: Ask if normal software could solve it effectively.
4. EVALUATE AI VALUE ADD: Ask if AI would provide additional value.
In our case: AI adds genuine value if matching user intent with video content requires deep semantic understanding that standard search 
algorithms cannot provide.
THE GOLDEN RULE FOR AI PRODUCT ENGINEERING
Do not use AI simply because AI is available. Always put the problem first, and AI 
second.

10-Step Checklist for Evidence-Driven Product Engineering
01. Who is the user?
02. What is the user trying to achieve?
03. What did the user actually do?
04. What do we know?
05. What are we assuming?
06. What problem might exist?
07. What evidence supports it?
08. What opportunity might exist?
09. What solutions could address it?
10. Would AI genuinely add value?
Keep this checklist handy whenever you are tasked with building a new feature.

Exercise: Scenario Analysis
Fresh Scenario
A user searches "How to prepare for a technical interview", opens several videos, skips through them, and leaves without 
watching a complete video.
01. Context & Evidence
User: Job seeker / candidate.
Goal: Quickly find relevant, actionable 
technical interview guidance.
Observed Behavior: Search → Open multiple 
videos → Skip/scrub → Early bounce.
What We Know: Low completion rate & rapid 
scrubbing signal high user friction.
What We Don't Know: Exact drop-off driver 
(poor intro, wrong topic depth, or bad 
audio/pacing?.
02. Problem & Opportunity
Possible Problem: Videos lack clear 
structure, forcing users to manually 
hunt for answers buried inside long 
intros.
Possible Opportunity: Provide 
immediate visual chaptering or direct 
key takeaway highlights upfront.
Possible Solution: Timestamped topic 
jump markers, bite-sized Q&A clips, or 
interactive transcript indexing.
03. AI Leverage
Could AI Help? YES — high strategic 
fit.
Why & How:
• Automatically transcribe & parse 
video content into key question 
blocks.
• Match exact user query intent 
directly to video timestamps.
• Generate dynamic short summaries 
so users evaluate relevance instantly.
Closing Takeaway
Don't start with "What should we build?" Start with "What is happening, why, and what evidence do we 
have?"

Thank You!

FDE Work Cycle & Project Lifecycle — Discussion Notes 
Forward Deployed Engineer (FDE) 
Work Cycle 
1. What is an FDE? 
A Forward Deployed Engineer (FDE) works closely with customers to understand real-world business 
problems, design and build technical or AI solutions, deploy them into the customer's environment, and 
remain focused on whether the solution produces a useful outcome. 
2. FDE Work Cycle 
The FDE Work Cycle describes how an FDE continuously works through customer problems. It is a 
repeating cycle rather than a one-time project process.

2. Define the right problem Turn the business pain into a

3. Design the AI/technical 
approach 
Decide what the system should 
do, what data is needed, how it 
should integrate, and how 
success will be measured. 
Plan the solution. 
4. Build within real constraints Build using the customer's real 
data, systems, infrastructure, 
security, and operational 
constraints. 
Build something usable in reality. 
5. Deploy into production Move the solution from prototype 
to the live environment where 
real users and data are involved. 
Make it work for real users. 
6. Own outcomes and improve Monitor the system, fix failures, 
learn from real usage, and 
improve the solution. 
Measure, improve, and repeat. 
3. Example: Customer Requests an AI Chatbot 
Customer request: “Build us an AI chatbot.” 
A typical development approach may begin by asking about chatbot features. 
An FDE investigates first: 
• Why does the customer need a chatbot? 
• What actual problem are employees or customers experiencing? 
• Is AI really the best solution? 
• What data and systems must the solution access? 
• How will success be measured? 
• Can the solution be deployed safely into the customer's environment? 
The FDE then builds, deploys, observes real usage, and improves the system. The important point is that 
the FDE does not simply implement the customer's first requested solution. 
4. Problems FDEs Face During the Work Cycle 
FDEs face more than coding problems. They commonly deal with customer, business, data, integration, 
security, deployment, adoption, evaluation, and continuous-improvement problems.

5. Five Major FDE Challenges to Remember 
1. The customer may not clearly know what problem should be solved. 
2. The data required to build a useful AI solution may be unavailable or low quality. 
3. The AI solution must connect to existing software, databases, APIs, and infrastructure. 
4. A model that works in a demo or notebook may not work reliably in a real production environment. 
5. Customers may expect AI to solve everything, so the FDE must set realistic expectations.
